description:
FOUND s494 (Fable, 2026-09-21) by the ENDURANCE battery (Q4; ~/pcl-agent-scratch/s494/q4/cases/e04-streval-same.pl, run1a.log: checkpoints every 25k are evenly spaced -- 13 / 27 / 42 / 57 s -- so the cost is per execution and constant, not growth; RSS 91 -> 96 MB).
MECHANISM (read, cl/pcl-runtime.lisp `%p-eval-1`): `*p-eval-string-cache*` maps (text, package, features, capture names) -> the transpiled CL TEXT; the body then does "READ+EVAL form-by-form (like `load`)" on every execution -- its comment explains why the READ is per form (an `(in-package …)` inside the text must take effect before the next form is read).  SBCL's `eval` in the default `:compile` evaluator mode runs the native compiler on each form: that is the half millisecond.  NOT measured: the split between read, compile and run (a 3-minute sb-sprof of the loop is the first thing a fixer does).
WHY IT MATTERS: `eval $string` inside a loop or a hot sub is how data-driven Perl is written (a dispatch table of code strings, a config-driven filter `eval $rule`, `eval "require $module"` per call, Try::Tiny-less guards) -- and string eval is a HARD USER REQUIREMENT of this project ("must be supported", memory project_dynamic_eval_is_required).  The first execution's cost (transpile) is understood and cached twice over; the steady-state cost was never measured because no bench row evals the same string twice.
FIX SHAPE: cache the COMPILED artefact beside the text -- for a cache key whose text has been read once, keep the list of (form-package . compiled thunk) pairs: each top-level form compiled ONCE as `(lambda () FORM)` in the package it was read in, and re-execution = funcall the thunks in order under the same dynamic bindings the eval path establishes today (*package*, *p-eval-lex-alist*, the location scope).  The capture ALIST is looked up at RUN time by name (p-eval-thunk's free-name resolution; s387's key rule already makes the key cover the capture NAMES), so a compiled thunk is reusable across executions with DIFFERENT captured values -- VERIFY with the probe `for my $i (1..3) { my $x = $i * 10; print eval q{$x + 1}, "\n" }` (11 21 31) and the five-row #296-B1 acceptance table.  Forms that must NOT be frozen: anything whose READ has side effects on later forms is already handled by reading once in order; `eval-when` / defmacro-defining text -- measure whether emitted eval text ever contains one; a `BEGIN` inside the eval string must run on EVERY execution (perl compiles per execution: `eval q{BEGIN { $n++ } 1}` three times -> $n == 3 -- PROBE what PCL does today first; if today's answer is already 3 the thunk list must keep that).
 Alternative, cheaper and partial: bind `sb-ext:*evaluator-mode*` to `:interpret` for SMALL texts (sb-eval has no compile step) -- measure both; the interpreter is slow for loops inside the eval'd text, so a size / shape test would be needed.  Prefer the thunk cache.
WHAT COULD BREAK: redefinition semantics (`eval "sub f { 1 }"` then `eval "sub f { 2 }"` are different keys -- fine; the SAME text re-executed re-installs the same definition -- fine); `local` / `our` declarations inside the text; `__LINE__` / `(eval N)` numbering (N counts executions -- the counter is outside the text, keep it); the eval DISK cache (#1200) is orthogonal (it stores text).
BAR: a bench row `evalloop` added to tools/bench-exec.pl (verified against perl); e04 before -> after; Pl/t/eval-01.t + state-eval-01.t + the eval rows of the sweep (perl-tests/eval.t by ROWS); companion op/eval.t, op/evalbytes.t, comp/ (`--jobs 1`); full sweep (cl/ change); ir-spec's eval section gets the statement "the emitted text of a string eval is compiled once per cache key".
SIZE: half an agent-day; a perf-round member (candidate for the round after #2098).
subject: Target-A, string eval in a LOOP: re-executing an ALREADY-CACHED eval string costs 0.57 ms -- 100,000 x `eval "2 + 3"` = 57.7 s under pcl, 0.31 s under perl (186x); the in-memory cache holds the emitted CL TEXT, so every execution READS the text again and hands each form to SBCL's `eval`, which COMPILES it again
